Definition
In the previous lessons on microprocessors, you learned about basic microprocessor operation and the three basic elements found in microprocessors, the registers, the ALU, and the control section.
INTRODUCTIONM
In this lesson, you will study the 8086 microprocessor in detail. You will learn about the internal structure of the 8086 microprocessor, including the registers, ALU, and the control sections.

You will also learn about the input/output signals present at each pin of the 8086 IC package. These signals are used to control the external microprocessor system elements and to transfer data between the microprocessor and the rest of the system.
After completing this lesson, you will be able to describe the structure and unique features of the 8086.
Let's begin the lesson on 8086 MICROPROCESSOR CIRCUIT.....................
LESSON MENU
The 8086 is a 16 bit microprocessor. The internal registers and data buses are 16 bits wide. The external data bus of the 8086 microprocessor is also 16 bits wide.
DISCUSSION
The 8086 has a 20 bit address bus and thus the 8086 can address up to 2 or 1M (1,048,576) bytes of memory. However, the internal address registers of the 8086 are only 16 bits.
For this reason, special registers known as segment registers are used. These will be covered in more detail later in this lesson.
The 8086 can also address up to 65,000 16 bit I/O ports. Parallel ports, serial ports, keyboards, and LCDs are just a few of the devices that can be attached to these I/O ports.
Sometimes more than one port address is required for a device. This is why there are so many to use.

Basically, the 8086 is compatible with the 8088, 80286, 80386, 80486 and Pentium Processors. All of these processors do have similarities. The farther up the list you go, the more additions to the basic design.
Understanding the operation of the 8086 will allow you to understand the operation of the more complex models of this family. Let's look at an internal block diagram of the 8086.
The functional diagram of the 8086 is shown below..........

You can see from the diagram that the sections of the 8086 microprocessors are connected by internal busses. All communications within the microprocessor are performed by the combined effort of the data and control bus.
The address bus is primarily for addressing locations or devices external to the internal system. The data bus of the 8086 is 16 bits wide. This is why the 8086 is known as a 16 bit processor.

The operation of these elements must be coordinated by the control sections of the microprocessor. The microprocessor performs many operations for each instruction that is executed.

In addition to the actions that were listed for the addition instruction, the microprocessor must also check the status of the interrupts, hold, reset and ready signals while executing the instruction.

Now that you have an idea of what steps the microprocessor must perform for a basic instruction, let's look at the sections of the 8086 microprocessor in detail. It is here that you will see a breakdown of each element and how they interface with one another.

Registers are where data and addresses are temporarily stored within the microprocessor. The data in the registers can be accessed and changed much faster than data in external memory IC's. Let's look at a brief summary of each register.
The accumulator (AX register) is used for arithmetic, logic, load and store operations. The accumulator can be accessed as a 16 bit register by using AX, or as two 8 bit registers as AL and AH.

The L and H stand for Low and High. You cannot add an 8 bit value to a 16 bit value, only 8 to 8 and 16 to 16. If you are trying to add a 8 bit value to a 16 bit value, you must set the other 8 bits to zero and then do a 16 bit add.
The BX (base), CX (counter), and DX (data) registers are general purpose registers that can be used for anything. The names given to these are normally used as a convention.

If you had a counter in a program, using the CX register for the counter data would make your code more readable, however, any of the registers can be used. Just as with the accumulator, these registers can be read as 16 bit BX, CX, DX or 8 bit, BL, BH, CL, CH, DL and DH.

The stack pointer (SP) is a special address register that always points to the location in memory of the top of the stack. A stack is a block of memory where data is stored like a stack of papers. You must take papers off the stack to see what is below them.

The base pointer (BP), source index (SI) and destination index (DI) are also address registers used for specific purposes. The base pointer normally points to the beginning of data in memory, where the index address registers are used in manipulating strings in memory.

The instruction pointer always points to the memory location of the next instruction to be executed. The registers always contain a 16 bit address. This 16 bit address is used with the segment registers to actually denote the location in external memory.
The flag register contains 9 bits which indicate certain conditions within the system.
The segment registers are used to indicate segments of memory. Even though the 8086 can use up to 1 Megabyte of memory, it is separated into 64 Kilobyte segments.
This means that address registers within the 8086 can only indicate a location within 64 kilobytes. For this reason, the segment registers contain a 16 bit value indicating the segment.
When the actual address is determined, the first four bits of the segment value are always zero, and the other 16 are the 16 bits in the segment register.
Then the offset address from an address register is added to it. Address registers are the pointer, index registers and the instruction pointer. This results in a 20 bit address.
Also, not shown, are internal buffers which are used to temporarily hold data or addresses that are exchanged with the address and data buses.

Data is transferred between registers or between a register and another section of the microprocessor on the internal data bus. The timing and control block regulates the flow of data within the microprocessor.

The arithmetic/logic unit (ALU) of the 8086 microprocessor performs all arithmetic and logic operations for the system. The ALU can add, subtract, increment, decrement, AND, OR, XOR, compare, rotate and complement.
Depending on the conditions of the results, certain flags will be set in the FLAG register. These can indicate problems within an operation. An example would be a carry in addition.
If the values you add result in a number larger than 16 bits can show, a carry flag is generated. This indicates that the number actually has an additional bit in the 17th slot.
When using a 16 bit addition to add 32 bits, the second addition of the upper two words has to know about the carry.
Other arithmetic commands are created from these basic operations. Even multiplication and division can be done with these simple arithmetic and logic functions.
The graphic below illustrates an example of an addition within the accumulator. The instruction decoder has told the ALU (via the control section) that the pending operation is an addition.

When all of the data has been moved into place, the control register instructs the ALU to perform the operation. The result is then placed in a location dictated by the instruction and the control section. The FLAGS of the FLAG register are adjusted according to the result.

The timing and control block includes the circuitry to apply the internal clock signals, process the READY, HOLD and RESET signals, and generate the memory I/O control signals. Each of these signals will be examined in greater detail later in this lesson.
TIMING AND CONTROL
The HLDAK and HLDRQ signals are used for something known as Direct Memory Access (DMA). This is where a device other than the microprocssor takes control of the data and address bus.
This is for situations where high speed data transfer is needed. The other device could even be a second microprocessor in your system.

The READY signal is typically generated by slow memory and I/O devices to tell the microprocessor that the device is ready to send or receive data. If the memory cannot supply data in the required number of clock signals, it holds the READY line LOW until the data is on the data bus.
This slows down overall operation of the system because the microprocessor is usually idle while the READY line is low. This type of memory access is known as asynchronous.

Asynchronous means that the microprocessor is unsure how long the memory will take to be ready. In a synchronous system, the memory is always faster than the microprocessor so the READY signal is not needed.

The status control signals are used to tell external circuitry what the microprocessor is doing. This section is always used in conjunction with the control section when managing the operation of external circuits.
In the next lesson you will see the importance of these signals to the proper movement of information from external devices to the microprocessor and vice versa.
If the timing is incorrect, devices may begin conflicting with one another, generating erroneous results. Now let's look at the interrupt control section.
This block allows the microprocessor to stop what it is doing and service an external device, such as a keyboard.
INTERRUPT
Without interrupts, the currently executing program would have to repeatedly check or poll each external device to ensure readiness for data transfer.
For example, when you press a key on the keyboard of personal computer, an interrupt is generated. The computer stops executing the current program and stores the keystroke in a buffer.

The computer then continues execution of the program. The NIDA 8086 microprocessor card set does not use an interrupt for the keyboard. Rather, the keyboard circuits are continually polled to see if a key has been pressed. There are advantages and disadvantages to both methods.

When the microprocessor receives an interrupt, the current operation is halted. It then executes another program to specifically deal with that interrupt. After processing the interrupt, the microprocessor returns to the program it was executing when the interrupt occurred.

When the microprocessor receives an interrupt request, the device generating the interrupt must place a value on the data bus. This value indicates the type of interrupt requested. There are 255 different interrupts that the 8086 can handle.

All of these interrupts can be ignored by certain settings in the 8086. The non-maskable interrupt (NMI) is the only one that cannot be prevented from occurring. NMI interrupts are normally reserved for extremely important processor external conditions.

When an interrupt is called, the interrupt program must do several things so the original program register settings are correct when program execution resumes. The list below indicates the minimum number of steps that must be performed by the interrupt program: Graphic Text) 1. Save the contents of any general purpose register that will be changed during the interrupt routine. 2. Service the cause of the interrupt. 3. Restore the contents of the registers. 4. Issue a RETURN instruction.w
1. Save the contents of any general purpose register that will be changed during the interrupt routine.
3. Restore the contents of the registers.
d. Moves the result back to the Accumulator.

These steps provide for correct interrupt recovery. If you modified registers and didn't restore them to their proper values, errors would likely exist in the main program data after you begin running it again.

Now that we have looked at the internal sections, let's look at the pin-out of the 8086 microprocessor. from these pins at the proper time during operation. Having two signals on one line is known as multiplexing.

The pin configuration of the 8086 is shown below. Note that address pins 0 through 15 are also the data pins. Special circuitry will take the correct information from these pins at the proper time during operation. Having two signals on one line is known as multiplexing.

The signal names assigned to the pins may differ from one manufacturer to another. The functions, however, remain identical. The pin-out is representative of the NEC V30 chip used by the Nida PC130-410.
*Parenthesized signal names are for the V30 in large scale applications.
HLRDQ (RQ/AK0)
HLDAK (RQ/AK1)
WR (BUSLOCK)
Pin 1 is used for tests conducted at the factory. This pin should be held at ground potential for normal opertions. Pin 20 is the IC's system ground.
Pins 2-16 & 39 (AD0 - AD15) are the multiplexed Address/Data Bus. In a machine cycle this bus is the address bus first, then it becomes the data bus for the remainder of the cycle.
Pin 17 (NMI) is the Non-Maskable Interrupt. This input is for an interrupt which cannot be ignored by the microprocessor. The other interrupt types can be "masked" out.
Pin 18 (INT) is the Interrupt Request. This is a general purpose interrupt that the microprocessor can choose to ignore.

Pin 19 (CLK) is the Clock. This pin is connected to a clock signal generating device which is set to a frequency which the microprocessor can operate at. In most cases, the 8284 Clock generator is used to provide the clock signal.

Pin 21 (RESET) is the Reset input. When this signal is set high, the microprocessor is reset and the instruction pointer is set to zero. The RESET signal can also be provided by the 8284 Clock generator.

Pin 22 (READY) is the Ready input. If ready is high during a read or write cycle, it indicates that the memory or peripheral is ready to send or receive data, low indicates it's not ready. This signal is also supplied by the 8284 Clock Generator.
Pin 23 is the POLL pin which is used in external synchronization with the microprocessor.

Pin 24 (INTAK) This output is the Interrupt Acknowledge. The INTAK signal is used instead of the RD signal during the instruction cycle after an interrupt request is accepted. It indicates to the requesting device that the interrupt has been acknowledged.
HLRDQ (RQ/AK0)
HLDAK (RQ/AK1)
WR (BUSLOCK)

Pin 25 (ASTB) is the Address Strobe. The address latch consists of a bank of flip-flops used to store the last input value. The address latch stores the address from the multiplexed lines so it will be available for the rest of the cycle. The address strobe tells the address latch it can take the information on the A/D pins.

Pin 26 (BUFEN) is the Output Buffer Enable. A buffer is used to add power to data from the data bus to other locations in a system. The 8086 data bus does not have enough power to push the data out to external devices. A buffer amplifies the data signals. This pin enables that buffer.

Pin 27 (BUFR/W) is the Output Buffer Read/Write. Buffers can only amplify in one direction, unless a bi-directional buffer is used, also known as a transceiver. This means the direction of data flow through the buffer has to be specified by an external signal to the buffer. This signal from the microprocessor provides that signal to the buffer.
Pin 28 (IO/M) is the Input/Output or Memory Selector. It indicates to external devices that the microprocessor is trying to access memory or an external I/O device.
Pin 29 (WR) is the Write Strobe. A low level indicates the data on the data bus is to be written to the selected memory address or I/O location.
WR (BUSLOCK)
Pin 30 (HLDAK) is the Hold Acknowledge. This indicates that the microprocessor has received a hold request and will relinquish the bus in the next clock cycle.
HLDAK (RQ/AK1)

Pin 31 (HLDRQ) is the Hold Request. This indicates that another device is requesting the use of the address and data buses. The address, data, RD, WR, and IO/M line are set to high impedance. This means they are theoretically not connected to the microprocessor. This allows the other device to put its signals on those lines.
HLRDQ (RQ/AK0)
Pin 32 (RD) is the Read Strobe. A low level indicates the selected memory or I/O device is to be read and that the data bus is available for data transfer.
HLDAK (RQ/AK1)
WR (BUSLOCK)

Pin 33 (S/LG) is the Minimum or Maximum Mode, also known as small and large mode. This indicates whether an external bus control device is being used. If so, then the bus control pins have a different purpose on the 8086 microprocessor.
All pins described in this lesson are for small mode which means the internal bus controller is being used. The 8086 has numerous functions, just not enough pins for all of them.
Pin 34 (UBE) is the Upper Bus Enable otherwise known as the High Bus Enable.

Pins 35-39 (A16-A20) are also for the Address Bus. The most significant 4 bits are the memory or I/O address. If the microprocessor was used in large mode, these pins also provide multiplexed status signals to the bus controller. The Nida 8086 Microprocessor is not used in this way.
Pin 40 (Vdd) is for Power. The power used by the 8086 microprocessor is provided by a +5 volt supply.
As you begin to learn more about the interface between the microprocessor and external circuitry, the purpose for these signals will become more apparent.
In the experiment, you will be able to look at any of these signals and compare them with other signals in the system.

15. Press the RESET button on the PC130-410 card. You will be entering a program into memory for execution by the microprocessor.
Entering programs into memory of the 8086 uses the EDIT function of the Monitor Program. Once you have pressed EDIT, you will be asked to enter an address.

There are two ways to enter an address, just a segment or a segment with an offset. For example, 2000: and 2000:0 or 2000:0000 are all the same location. In this experiment we will start our program at segment 2000, with an offset of zero.

After you enter a value like "2000:", the code editor program will begin. The top part of the screen will show the segment you are in. The bottom part of the screen will show the current offset and the 8 bit value stored at that offset.

There are three things you can do at any offset and any segment. Enter a new value and press enter, press the down arrow to move to the next offset, or use the up arrow to move to the previous offset.
Every time you enter a value and press enter, you will automatically move to the next offset. If, at anytime, you press enter without entering data, zeros will be loaded at that memory location.
Remember to use the up and down arrows for movement through your code. When a program is shown to you, you will be given an address, opcodes, mnemonic and a description.

You start at the first address given and enter each opcode consecutively into memory until you are finished entering the program. The mnemonic is what an assembler program would use to generate the opcodes for a program.
Once you are finished entering your program, press STOP. To verify that your program is loaded, press the DISPLAY R.M. key and enter the starting address of the program.

After you press ENTER, all the opcodes for the location and the next 17 locations will be shown. Again, use the up and down arrows to move through memory. Notice that when the signal is applied, the HLDAK pin supplies a 5 Volts "1" to indicate it acknowledges the request and is allowing some other device to use the bus.
You can see that the processor stopped from the display of the Nida Demo program. Once you remove the request, the acknowledge goes away and the program begins right where it left off.

In other words, you requested control of the busses. The computer acknowledged and gave control to you. The microprocessor address, control and data lines went to high impedance effectively removing them from the external busses.

Entering programs into memory of the 8086 uses the EDIT function of the Monitor Program. Once you have pressed EDIT, you will be asked to enter an address.

There are two ways to enter an address, just a segment or a segment with an offset. For example, 2000: and 2000:0 or 2000:0000 are all the same location. In this experiment we will start our program at segment 2000, with an offset of zero.

After you enter a value like "2000:", the code editor program will begin. The top part of the screen will show the segment you are in. The bottom part of the screen will show the current offset and the 8 bit value stored at that offset.

There are three things you can do at any offset and any segment. Enter a new value and press enter, press the down arrow to move to the next offset, or use the up arrow to move to the previous offset.
Every time you enter a value and press enter, you will automatically move to the next offset. If, at anytime, you press enter without entering data, zeros will be loaded at that memory location.
Remember to use the up and down arrows for movement through your code. When a program is shown to you, you will be given an address, opcodes, mnemonic and a description.

You start at the first address given and enter each opcode consecutively into memory until you are finished entering the program. The mnemonic is what an assembler program would use to generate the opcodes for a program.
Once you are finished entering your program, press STOP. To verify that your program is loaded, press the DISPLAY R.M. key and enter the starting address of the program.

After you press ENTER, all the opcodes for the location and the next 17 locations will be shown. Again, use the up and down arrows to move through memory.
